This text is a field dispatch relating to the survey of the Bengal Nagpur railway extension. It was written at Chanda on 29 November 1889 by Mr. Reginald Shaw, the assistant engineer, and addressed to the chief engineer at Calcutta.

The dispatch reports that the survey party, which numbered 34 persons in total, including 12 chainmen and 6 sappers of the Madras Sappers, had completed the location survey of the 92-mile section running from Nagbhid to Chanda. This work was finished on 22 November, after fourteen weeks spent in the field.

As located, the line follows the Wyne Ganga valley for 41 miles, crosses that river by means of a bridge of seven spans, each 150 feet long, at Karanja, and then takes the northern flank of the hills.

Shaw estimates the earthwork for the whole section at 480,000 cubic yards, of which 62,000 cubic yards consist of rock excavation in the eleven miles beyond Ballarshah. For the crossing of the river at Karanja, three different alignments were examined. The line that was adopted is 1.7 miles longer than the southern route, but it avoids 90,000 cubic yards of rock excavation and two well sinkings.

The country between Ballarshah and Chanda is reported to be healthy, with the exception of the months of July and August, when fever caused the deaths of four chainmen during the season.

The party's expenses to date amounted to 19,400 rupees, set against a sanctioned grant of 30,000 rupees. In light of this, Shaw makes three requests: an additional 8,000 rupees to cover the next season; a theodolite to replace the one that was damaged at the Wyne Ganga crossing on 3 September; and the loan of a second survey elephant from the Chanda division, since the party's own elephant had gone lame after the monsoon.

Shaw closes the dispatch by noting that the levelling of the first 40 miles has been checked twice, and that the two checks agree with each other within 0.15 feet.

The text is a record of a British consular report concerning the wool trade of the La Plata region. The report was prepared in Buenos Aires by Her Majesty's Consul, Mr. Edmund Monson, and was sent to the Foreign Office on 20 April 1875.

According to the report, the wool clip for the season that had just ended was estimated at 68,000,000 pounds in weight, compared with 61,000,000 pounds the season before. The consul attributed this increase mainly to the spread of fencing across the estancias of the southern camps.

Of the total clip, about 26,000 bales were shipped to Havre, 19,000 bales went to Antwerp, and 11,500 bales were sent to Great Britain. Whatever remained was processed in local factories; the report noted that fourteen such factories were operating at the time, up from nine a year earlier.

The average price obtained at the sales was elevenpence per pound for greasy wool, which represented a decline of twopence farthing compared with the previous year. The consul also recorded that the S.A. Bienvenida sheep, first introduced by the Sociedad Rural in 1868, had by the most reliable estimates reached a total of 3,000,000 head, and that the wool from these sheep commanded a premium of one penny per pound above the ordinary criollo clip.

The report gave figures for transport and insurance costs: freight to London was quoted at five eighths of a penny per pound, while freight to Havre was a halfpenny farthing per pound; insurance on consignments to London ran at thirty-five shillings per cent.

Finally, the report closed with two observations about local improvements. The drainage of the flood-prone lands near Dolores, a project begun in 1873 under the direction of the engineer Mr. James Baine, had reclaimed approximately 400 square miles of pasture. In addition, the railway running from Tandil to the port, which had opened on 1 February of that year, had already succeeded in lowering cartage charges by two shillings per bale.

This text is the log of the whaler Diana of Hull, kept by the ship's surgeon, Dr. Charles Edward Smith, during the Davis Strait fishery of 1866. The Diana was a brig-rigged steam whaler of 350 tons register, commanded by Captain John Gravill. She left Hull on 12 February with a crew of 49 hands. Of these, 8 were green hands — inexperienced men — shipped at a wage of two pounds ten shillings per month, while the seasoned men drew three pounds five shillings.

The ship crossed the Arctic Circle on 3 March, in longitude 22 degrees west, and made the ice edge off Disko on 19 March. The first whale was struck on 2 April off the Women's Islands and yielded 12 tons of oil and 9 hundredweight of bone. A second whale, taken on 17 April, yielded 15 tons. By the end of May, the catch stood at four whales and 1,400 seals.

On 11 June, the ship was nipped in the ice in Melville Bay and lost her rudder. The carpenter fashioned a temporary rudder from spare spars within three days. The vessel was then beset and drifted with the pack ice for 61 days. During this drift, the surgeon recorded the first case of scurvy on 8 July, and by the middle of August, 22 men were on the sick list. The ship's supply of lime juice had run out, so when the ship touched land on 21 August, the crew ate sorrel gathered on the Greenland coast. Three men died in the last week of August and were buried on shore.

The Diana worked free of the ice on 25 September and reached Hull on 11 October with 41 tons of oil and 3 tons of bone. The voyage was a paying one only because of the seal catch. The owners, Samuel and Charles Gourlay, declared the gross earnings at 3,860 pounds and paid each seasoned hand 19 pounds twelve shillings for the voyage.
